newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Penalties on Nomura, DKB.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Penalties on Nomura, DKB.

text.p: Below are analysts' initial comments on administrative penalties against Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Ltd (DKB) for their involvement in a racketeer payoff scandal. The Finance Ministry on Wednesday announced the penalties which included suspension of some key business at both institutions.
PAUL HEATON, ANALYST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:
On Nomura: "I'm assuming Nomura won't make profits for the next two quarters but that may be too pessimistic."

"However, once the sanctions are behind them, they will be making a very concerted effort to say we're good and clean and I don't think it will take more than a few months to get back their clients. If they started losing a lot of staff, that would be a different story."

On DKB: "The biggest impact is on the domestic reputation of the company, that's the difficulty for them. If people close accounts as a result, it would take many years to get them back. But I don't think that is going to happen."
"On the loan side, it doesn't affect existing client it's even less of an impact than Nomura."
Commenting on an order to suspend new business overseas until August 1998, he said, "Most overseas business has not been very profitable for them in common with other Japanese banks."
BRIAN WATERHOUSE, FINANCIAL ANALYST, HSBC JAMES CAPEL:

Concerning Nomura: "It is rather less severe than originally feared. At most, this could cut Nomura's profits by one-third but it is certainly not going to cause insurmountable losses and who knows? It has already led to major changes in management so in the long-term it could be quite beneficial for the company as an entity."

"I think Nomura's clients will come back, but it could take considerable time. Nomura is a very powerful company and it's one that can't be ignored. So ultimately, while they've been put in the 'sin-bin' (punished)...I think clients will start to come back."

Concerning DKB: "A suspension til the end of the year of new loans, given the environment in which there is very weak loan demand, there will be some impact but...I think any negative impact in profits will be limited."

On the suspension of DKB's new business overseas until August 1998, he said: "Certainly it will put a dent in their business especially since they have been pursuing syndicated loans in Southeast Asia."

Waterhouse said that the ministry's decision to exempt housing loans from the suspension to avoid penalising individuals had reduced the impact of the punishment by excluding the area for which there was greatest loan demand.
"I think overall, the impact on DKB should be fairly minimal."
JESPER KOLL, CHIEF ECONOMIST, J.P. MORGAN, TOKYO:
On Nomura: "The suspension of proprietary trading is like having their right arm ripped off -- it's about a quarter of their profits."
"It hurts their profits over the next year, but in terms of the 'Big Bang,' it forces them to restructure more aggressively. I think the only question is whether they can contain the human capital."
"It opens a window of opportunity for any company with a good fiduciary track record (to take business away from Nomura). Who is that? No Japanese companies spring to mind."

Concerning DKB: "They're starting from a very, very strong position in the domestic loan market and if they are out of syndicated loans for six months, it's a similarly severe punishment, but I think the overall impact will be that it forces them to rethink and restructure."
DOMESTIC BROKERAGE ANALYST, who declined to be identified:

Concerning Nomura: "The suspension of dealing for six months is not such a big minus, but...Nomura's previous corporate clients -- who have already started to defect -- will probably not come back and the impact of that will be great."
"The scandal is likely to spread to Yamaichi, Daiwa and Nikko and the clients who defect from the Big Four will go to foreign houses, not domestic brokerages."
"This is likely to speed up the reorganisation of the securities industry, and domestic brokerages are likely to tie up or merge with foreign houses or domestic banks."

A FINANCIAL INDUSTRY ANALYST AT A RESEARCH INSTITUTE AFFILIATED TO A SECOND-TIER JAPANESE BROKERAGE WHO DECLINED TO BE IDENTIFIED: On Nomura: "The penalties imposed on Nomura were within our expectations, except for the suspension of stock broking at all branches for a week."

"The suspension at all branches could directly hit individual investors and we need to know more precisely about what the penalty really is and we need to assess what its impact on Nomura's business will be like."

"But, Nomura is far stronger than other brokerages in the Japanese securities industry, so it is unlikely that it will lose its competitiveness due to the partial business suspension announced today."

On DKB: "The situation is different for DKB. It is not the strongest in the banking industry. The suspension from starting new businesses for one year could severely affect the bank's business, in particular, its services for individual customers."
